title: Topology is not silent in the transport noise of multiband bosons
abstract: For electrons at a Fermi surface, the topological part of the Berry curvature drops out of the transport noise: the anomalous Hall conductivity is quantized, and the fluctuations of the Hall current know nothing about the Chern number. We show that this cancellation is an accident of the Fermi surface, and that it fails for bosons. Magnons and phonons thermally populate every band, each with its own Chern number, so the harmonic sector of the Hodge decomposition of the curvature is not a single constant and a variance does not annihilate it. What survives is the occupation-weighted dispersion of Chern numbers across populated bands. That band geometry is visible in current noise is known, and at zero temperature the antisymmetric part of the noise sum rule already returns a Chern number; what is new is an object with no zero-temperature analogue, existing only when several bands are populated and weighted differently. We derive it from a fluctuating Boltzmann equation and settle the energy-magnetization subtraction at the level of fluctuations: the subtracted term is the curl of a bounded magnetization density, so it contributes exactly zero to the current any transport measurement records, realization by realization. Is the quantity measurable? A driven protocol is not: the excess noise sits twelve orders below the equilibrium floor. An equilibrium protocol is, through a sum rule on the antisymmetric part of the current cross-spectrum, which carries no drive and hence no suppression. We prove that the frequency-integrated form of that sum rule cannot separate the topological from the geometric content, and show that the frequency-resolved cross-spectrum does separate them at accessible resolution. The protocol is specified for Cu(1,3-bdc), with its robustness to nuisance-model completeness and to dispersion, thermometry and field calibration.
summary: This paper shows that unlike electrons where topological contributions to transport noise cancel out, multiband bosons retain a measurable topological signature in their current noise. This signature is captured by the occupation-weighted dispersion of Chern numbers across populated bands. The authors propose a frequency-resolved cross-spectrum measurement as the necessary protocol to isolate this topological signal.
main_problem: The paper investigates the topological contribution to the transport noise in multiband bosonic systems, contrasting this behavior with the known case for electrons at a Fermi surface.
main_result: The topological contribution to the noise is not canceled for bosons because the Berry curvature is band-dependent, leading to a measurable quantity: the occupation-weighted dispersion of Chern numbers across populated bands.
method: The analysis uses a fluctuating Boltzmann equation approach and examines the current cross-spectrum, proving that frequency resolution is necessary to separate topological from geometric content.
model_or_system: The model involves multiband bosons, such as magnons or phonons, whose band structure is analyzed using the Hodge decomposition of the Berry curvature two-form on the Brillouin zone.
key_observables: Current noise spectrum, frequency-resolved cross-spectrum, and the occupation-weighted dispersion of Chern numbers.
important_parameters: Temperature (finite-temperature effects are crucial), band occupation numbers, and frequency resolution ($\omega$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the failure of the cancellation mechanism observed in Fermi surface electrons, and it relies on developing a fluctuating Boltzmann equation framework.
figures_summary: The notes do not describe specific figures, but mention Table I showing the magnitude of the topological share of the noise variance for a kagome ferromagnet.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by decomposing the Berry curvature, contrasts the electronic (Fermi surface) case with the bosonic case, derives the noise calculation from a fluctuating Boltzmann equation, and concludes by specifying the necessary frequency-resolved measurement protocol.
why_interesting: The work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for detecting topological invariants in thermal noise measurements, which is a key area bridging topology, transport, and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
